newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - ranges seen before CPI.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - ranges seen before CPI.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market's Friday optimism should continue next week, but analysts see range trading until Wednesday's report on consumer prices.
The September consumer price index (CPI) will be the first course in a full menu of key economic data in the days ahead.
"The CPI is going to keep a lid on things probably in near term," said economist Lee Youngdahl at Aubrey G. Lanston.
"Then assuming that doesn't come out on the negative side we'll probably press the top end of the range ... because the other releases are supposed to be pretty benign," he added.
Treasuries rallied across the curve on Friday, after the release of September producer price and retail sales data.

But trading should be cautious early next week. The 30-year bond should remain incarcerated between rangepoints, with a 7.0 percent yield defining the bottom of the trading range and 6.75 percent setting the top, analysts said.
After Friday's data the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond surged nearly three-quarters of a point. Its yield fell as low as 6.83 percent, down from 6.89 percent at the open.
The producer price index (PPI) rose 0.2 percent in September and 0.3 percent less food and energy.
In August the PPI rose 0.3 percent with the core rate falling 0.1 percent.
Forecasters polled by Reuters expected the overall PPI to rise 0.3 percent, and core PPI to increase 0.2 percent.

And even though retail sales rose a larger-than-expected 0.7 percent in September, the numbers were weaker than they appeared on the surface, which should support bonds and keep yields from rising early next week, analysts said.
The September sales gain was offset by tepid sales in August, which were revised downward to show a decline of 0.2 percent, from a rise of 0.2 percent originally.
"I thought the numbers were pretty constructive," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.

Consumer prices are estimated to have risen at a faster rate in September than the 0.1 percent increase seen in both the overall and core rates in August, according to preliminary results of Reuters polling data.
Most economists polled so far forecast that retail prices overall rose between 0.3 percent and 0.4 percent in September, with many expecting core prices to rise by a similar amount.
"We're looking for trouble on those numbers," said Platt.
But Thursday data are likely to offer contradictory signals on the economy.
Industrial production is seen coming off the boil in September, after jumping 0.5 percent in August. The capacity utilization rate is seen slipping from 83.5 in August.
Housing starts are seen slackening in September from their 1.535-million unit annualized pace in August.
But the recent robustness of the housing sector could dash those preliminary forecasts, economists said.
"You also have the (Philadephia Federal Reserve Bank) manufacturing survey that day, which in my opinion is impossible to forecast," said Platt.
But experts said the index gives the first read on October manufacturing and could be important for the market.
On Friday analysts expect an international trade report to show the U.S. trade gap fell in July from $11.68 billion in August.
"They're going to have a lot of impact on third-quarter gross domestic product estimates," said Suzanne Rizzo, U.S. economist at MFR Inc. -- 212 859 1667
